title: Investors brace for results deluge
full_text:
Eighty per cent of ASX-listed companies are due to release earnings over the next fortnight, potentially blowing up a picture assembled so far of resilience in the face of macro-economic headwinds.
Analysts have trimmed their aggregate ASX 200 earnings forecast for the current financial year by 0.7 per cent – which is no more than the usual reporting season downgrade.
Even so, the ASX 200 had its worst week in four months last week, falling 1.6 per cent to 9115.19 points. Commonwealth Bank, Westpac and ANZ all flagged double-digit declines in mortgage applications after the tax changes announced in the May federal budget. That followed a 5.5 per cent rally over the previous fortnight, driven by gains in banks and resources.
Earnings downgrades for Transurban, CBA, SGH, Champion Iron, Beach Energy, Alcoa, Seek, Telstra, IAG and Newmont have been mostly offset by upgrades to ANZ, James Hardie, AGL, REA, AMP, Block, Treasury Wine, Charter Hall Retail REIT, Helia and News Corp, owner of this masthead.
“There are clear signs Australian households are reining in activity,” says MST senior analyst Hasan Tevfik. “The banks provide the most obvious evidence.” On top of the slump in mortgage applications, he points to CBA customers drawing down their savings.
Investors have heard from a cross-section of struggling households. Amotiv described soft demand in the RV and caravan market. REA witnessed weaker buyer inquiries late in the financial year, following the budget and rate rises. Telstra’s branded postpaid subscriber base fell by about 47,000 in the second half. Helia flagged softer mortgage demand and a double-digit fall in new lenders’ mortgage insurance premiums in the March quarter.
Yet consensus earnings per share forecasts for CBA and Westpac have fallen by less than 1 per cent, while ANZ forecasts have actually risen. Amotiv’s downgrade was only around 1.5 per cent, helped by its 4WD business. REA offset softer volumes with higher yield. Telstra did much the same through pricing, with mobile revenue rising despite weaker subscriber numbers. And despite softer mortgage demand, Helia reported that new delinquencies actually fell.
Mr Tevfik cautions there are “pockets of more serious weakness” in domestic demand, with Premier Investments and Myer both suffering material profit downgrades. “For now, though, they look more like exceptions than the rule,” he says. “Australian household demand is softening, but Australia Inc is proving much more resilient than consumers.” But UBS equity strategist Richard Schellbach cautions that while ASX 200 profit growth for the 2026 financial year is running at a respectable 11.7 per cent, it stands at just 5.5 per cent excluding mining and energy stocks.
“Although we are by no means in a profits recession, what we are seeing in Australia looks pedestrian compared to elsewhere,” he says. S&P 500 earnings growth is tracking near 50 per cent and Europe 22 per cent.
“With minimal exposure to AI and tech, the Australian equity market has become a spectator to what is an unprecedented boom in global profits.” Mr Schellbach expects the local earnings story to soften further over coming weeks as more small companies report. Outlook comments already tell “a cautious story” on the domestic consumer, citing worries about interest rates and the hit to confidence from the federal budget.
UBS remains underweight banks, consumer discretionary and real estate as a result.
Still, Mr Schellbach notes the “real” economic data looks OK. “Despite poor confidence, they are still spending,” he says of households. Dividend forecasts have been revised up by 0.4 per cent, with Treasury Wine, AMP, AGL and Computershare enjoying the biggest upgrades. Companies have also announced about $1.8bn of buybacks, led by Telstra and Suncorp. Karoon and Temple & Webster both unveiled buybacks in July worth up to 10 per cent of their shares on issue.
Mr Tevfik says buybacks are becoming essential armour against aggressive hedge funds. “Multi-manager hedge funds enter reporting season with plenty of leverage and abundant access to stock borrow. The pod shops (hedge funds) are effectively arriving with machine guns while many companies remain unarmed. A buyback can help level the battlefield.” Results from A2 Milk, Audinate, Aurizon, BlueScope Steel, GPT, Imdex, JB Hi-Fi, L1 Group, Lendlease, Iress, oOh!media, NAB and New Hope are due on Monday. The ASX 200 is expected to open down about 0.4 per cent, near 9080 points.
